title: How long can food stay out of the refrigerator?

seo.title: How long can food stay out of the refrigerator?
seo.meta_description: Perishable and cooked food should not sit at room temperature longer than 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F. Refrigerating or reheating later does not reset the risk.
seo.search_intent: Learn how long cooked and perishable foods can stay out, when they should be discarded, and why reheating does not always make them safe.

excerpt: As a general rule, cooked food and other perishables should not stay at room temperature for more than 2 hours. FDA shortens that limit to 1 hour when the air temperature is above 90°F (32°C). Once food has spent too long warm, putting it back in the refrigerator or reheating it does not erase bacterial growth or toxins that may already have formed.
content_html:
A casserole stays on the table after dinner, potato salad sits through an afternoon party, or a pot of stew cools on the counter for hours. In each case, the clock matters because bacteria grow much faster at warm temperatures than they do under refrigeration.

The general rule is 2 hours

FDA guidance says refrigerated perishables should not remain at room temperature for more than 2 hours. If they have been out longer and were not continuously kept cold or hot, the safe choice is to discard them.

You do not need to wait for a bad smell. Foodborne pathogens can multiply without creating an obvious change in odor, taste, or appearance.

Above 90°F, the limit drops to 1 hour

When the air temperature is above 90°F (32°C), FDA cuts the room-temperature window to one hour. A parked car, sunny picnic table, or area beside a grill can become hotter than the reported outdoor temperature.

A grocery bag on a car seat is not a cooler.

Which foods need this rule?

Meat, poultry, seafood, cooked eggs, refrigerated dairy, cooked rice and pasta, cooked beans, prepared meals, perishable sauces, deli salads, cut produce that requires refrigeration, and leftovers all belong in this category.

The rule does not apply in the same way to shelf-stable foods such as dry bread, nuts, uncooked rice, unopened canned goods, or whole produce that is normally stored at room temperature.

Keeping food cold or hot prevents the same clock from starting

Cold food should stay at 40°F (4°C) or below. Hot food being held for service should stay at 140°F (60°C) or above.

A safe buffet is not food sitting lukewarm for hours. It is food held genuinely cold or genuinely hot.

Putting it back in the refrigerator does not reset the time

If lasagna sits on the table for four hours, chilling it afterward only slows growth from that point forward. It does not remove bacteria that already multiplied or toxins some organisms may have produced.

Freezing works the same way. Cold preserves the state of the food; it does not turn poorly handled food back into fresh food.

Reheating is not a universal rescue

Thorough reheating kills many active bacteria. However, certain toxins formed during improper storage can survive heat. “I'll boil it later” is therefore not a reliable plan for food left out all afternoon.

The prevention step happens earlier: chill or refrigerate on time.

How to cool a large amount of food

Divide stew, pasta, rice, or cooked meat into shallow containers and smaller portions. They lose heat faster than a deep stockpot.

You do not need to wait for food to reach room temperature before refrigerating it. Modern refrigerators can handle reasonable portions of warm food; the goal is to avoid hours of slow cooling on the counter.

What if you do not know how long it has been out?

There is no household test that can reconstruct the missing time. Taking a small taste is not a safety test either.

For a perishable food with an unknown and potentially long period without temperature control, discarding it is the prudent choice.

The rule worth remembering

2 hours normally; 1 hour above 90°F. If food needs to be out longer, keep it continuously cold or hot.

Refrigeration and reheating preserve properly handled food; they do not erase several forgotten hours at room temperature.

faq.question: Can I eat food that sat out for 3 hours?
faq.answer: For perishable food, three hours exceeds FDA's general two-hour limit. Discard it if it was not continuously kept cold or hot.

faq.question: What if it is very hot outside?
faq.answer: The limit drops to one hour when the air temperature is above 90°F (32°C).

faq.question: Does reheating make food safe again?
faq.answer: Not always. Heat kills many bacteria, but some toxins can survive, and reheating does not erase unsafe storage history.
